content: The most effective pharmacological treatment for psychotic depression remains uncertain due to limited evidence. Current options include antidepressant monotherapy, antipsychotic monotherapy, mifepristone monotherapy, or a combination of an antidepressant and an antipsychotic. This review, updated from its previous versions in 2005 and 2015, aimed to evaluate the clinical efficacy of these treatments in patients with acute psychotic depression and to determine whether treatment response is influenced by prior non-response to other therapies. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, CCMDCTR, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, was conducted on February 21, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants with acute major depression with psychotic features were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, following Cochrane Handbook guidelines. The primary outcomes were clinical response (efficacy) and overall dropout rates (harm/tolerance). Secondary outcomes included remission of depression, changes in baseline severity scores, quality of life, and dropout rates due to adverse effects. The search yielded 3947 abstracts, but only 12 RCTs with 929 participants met the inclusion criteria. Due to clinical heterogeneity, meta-analyses were limited. The primary focus was on the reduction of depressive symptoms rather than psychotic symptoms. For antidepressant monotherapy, there was no significant difference in depression response compared to placebo (RR 8.40, 95% CI 0.50 to 142.27; very low-certainty evidence) or in overall dropout rates (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.34 to 4.51; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, antipsychotic monotherapy showed no significant difference in depression response compared to placebo (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.73; very low-certainty evidence) or in overall dropout rates (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.08; very low-certainty evidence). When comparing antidepressant monotherapy to antipsychotic monotherapy, no significant differences were observed in depression response (RR 2.09, 95% CI 0.64 to 6.82; very low-certainty evidence) or overall dropout rates (RR 1.79, 95% CI 0.18 to 18.02; very low-certainty evidence). However, lowto very low-certainty evidence suggests that combination therapy with an antidepressant and an antipsychotic may be more effective than antipsychotic monotherapy (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.40 to 2.38), antidepressant monotherapy (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.80), or placebo (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.82). There was no significant difference in overall dropout rates between combination therapy and antipsychotic monotherapy (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.01), antidepressant monotherapy (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.50), or placebo (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.18). No studies reported changes in depression severity from baseline, quality of life, or dropout rates due to adverse events. Additionally, no RCTs involving mifepristone met the inclusion criteria. The risk of bias across studies was significant, with variability in diagnostic criteria, randomization methods, treatment protocols, and outcome measures. In conclusion, psychotic depression remains an under-researched condition, limiting the reliability of current findings. Some evidence suggests that combination therapy with an antidepressant and an antipsychotic may be more effective than monotherapy or placebo. However, evidence supporting the efficacy of antidepressant or antipsychotic monotherapy is limited, and no evidence supports the use of mifepristone. Further high-quality research is needed to guide clinical practice.
